title: Introductory Microbiology — Bacteria and Viruses
topicTitle: Monera: General introduction, structure of bacterial cell, mode of nutrition, bacterial growth; cyanobacteria (blue green algae); Virus: General introduction, structure and importance of virus, bacteriophage
notes: **Bacteria:** prokaryotic, no nucleus, cell wall of peptidoglycan (Gram-positive thick, Gram-negative thin with outer membrane). Shapes: cocci, bacilli, spirilla, vibrio.
**Bacterial cell structure:** cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid (circular DNA), ribosomes (70S), plasmids (extrachromosomal DNA), capsule, flagella, pili.
**Nutrition:** autotrophic (photoautotrophs, chemoautotrophs) and heterotrophic (saprophytic, parasitic, symbiotic).
**Bacterial growth:** binary fission. Lag phase → log/exponential phase → stationary phase → death phase. Affected by temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients.
**Cyanobacteria:** photosynthetic prokaryotes with chlorophyll a and phycocyanin. Fix nitrogen (heterocysts in Anabaena). Form blooms in eutrophic water. Examples: Nostoc, Anabaena, Oscillatoria.
**Virus:** acellular, obligate intracellular parasite. Structure: nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) + protein coat (capsid) + sometimes lipid envelope.

**Bacteriophage:** virus that infects bacteria. T2 phage has icosahedral head, contractile tail. Lytic cycle: attachment, penetration, replication, assembly, lysis. Lysogenic cycle: phage DNA integrates into bacterial chromosome as prophage.

**Gram staining:** differential staining technique. Gram-positive bacteria retain crystal violet (appear purple) due to thick peptidoglycan. Gram-negative lose crystal violet and take up safranin (appear pink/red) due to thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane. Critical diagnostic tool.

**Bacterial shapes and arrangements:** cocci (spherical) — arranged as pairs (diplococci), chains (streptococci), clusters (staphylococci). Bacilli (rod-shaped) — single, pairs, or chains. Spirilla (spiral), vibrios (comma-shaped). Mycoplasma lack cell walls entirely.

**Bacterial reproduction:** binary fission (asexual, one cell splits into two identical cells). Generation time for E. coli is ~20 minutes under optimal conditions. Conjugation transfers plasmids between bacteria (horizontal gene transfer). Transformation takes up free DNA; transduction via bacteriophages.

**Bacterial endospores:** highly resistant dormant structures formed by some Gram-positive bacteria (Bacillus, Clostridium). Survive boiling, radiation, desiccation. Important in food preservation and medicine.

** Cyanobacteria ultrastructure:** photosynthesis occurs in thylakoid membranes (not in chloroplasts). Phycobilisomes on thylakoids capture light. Heterocysts have thick walls for nitrogen fixation (protects nitrogenase from oxygen). hormogonia are motile fragments for reproduction.

**Virus classification:** Baltimore classification based on nucleic acid type and replication strategy: Groups I-VI (DNA viruses), Group VII (pararetroviruses). Enveloped viruses (influenza, HIV) have lipid bilayer from host membrane. Naked viruses (adenovirus, poliovirus) lack envelope and are more environmentally stable.

**Virus structure details:** capsid proteins form geometric symmetry — icosahedral (spherical appearance), helical (rod-like), or complex (bacteriophages). Envelope contains viral glycoprotein spikes (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase in influenza). Genome can be single-stranded or double-stranded, linear or circular, segmented or non-segmented.

**Bacteriophage lifecycle details:** Lytic cycle: phage attaches via tail fibers to specific bacterial receptors, injects DNA, takes over host machinery, produces new phage components, assembles new virions, lyses cell with lysozyme. Lysogenic cycle: phage DNA integrates as prophage, replicates with host, can be induced to enter lytic cycle by stress (UV, chemicals).

**Viral host range:** specific to certain cell types. HIV infects CD4+ T cells (and macrophages) via CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 receptors. Influenza infects respiratory epithelial cells. Rhinovirus infects nasal epithelium. Host range determines disease symptoms and transmission.

**Viruses vs. living organisms:** viruses lack metabolism, cannot grow or respond to stimuli independently, and cannot reproduce without a host. They exist in a grey area between living and non-living. Giant viruses (Mimivirus, Pandoravirus) blur this line further with larger genomes and some metabolic genes.

**Important bacterial diseases:** tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella Typhi), pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae), tetanus (Clostridium tetani), botulism (Clostridium botulinum), leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae).
**Important viral diseases:** influenza, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B and C, rabies, polio, measles, common cold (rhinovirus), dengue, Zika, COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), smallpox (eradicated).

**Cyanobacteria ecological importance:** produce ~20-30% of Earth's oxygen through photosynthesis. Form symbiotic relationships with fungi (lichens), plants (Azolla fern), and corals. Fixed atmospheric nitrogen, enriching soils. Fossil cyanobacteria (stromatolites) are 3.5 billion years old — among Earth's earliest life forms.

**Bacterial cell wall chemistry details:** Peptidoglycan (murein) consists of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) cross-linked by peptide bridges. Gram-positive: 20-80 nm thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids (lipoteichoic acid anchors to membrane). Gram-negative: 2-7 nm peptidoglycan, outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (LPS = lipid A + core polysaccharide + O-antigen), porins for transport, periplasmic space with hydrolytic enzymes.

**Bacterial motility mechanisms:** Flagellar motion (peritrichous, polar, lophotrichous) driven by proton motive force (H+ gradient) rotating basal body. Gliding motility (myxobacteria, cyanobacteria) via type IV pili or slime secretion. Spirochetes have axial filaments (endoflagella) in periplasmic space causing corkscrew motion through viscous media.

**Bacterial nutrition expanded:** Photoautotrophs (cyanobacteria, purple/green sulfur bacteria) use light energy + CO2. Chemoautotrophs (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter, Thiobacillus) oxidize inorganic compounds (NH3, NO2-, H2S, Fe2+) for energy + CO2. Photoheterotrophs (purple non-sulfur bacteria) use light + organic carbon. Chemoheterotrophs (most pathogens, E. coli) use organic compounds for both energy and carbon. Parasitic nutrition harms host; symbiotic benefits both (e.g., Rhizobium-legume).

**Bacterial growth curve mathematical model:** N = N₀ × 2^(t/g) where N₀ = initial population, g = generation time. During log phase, growth rate is maximal and constant. Stationary phase: nutrient depletion, waste accumulation, secondary metabolite production (antibiotics). Death phase: exponential decline. Continuous culture (chemostat) maintains exponential growth by nutrient inflow/waste outflow at dilution rate D = μ (specific growth rate).

**Cyanobacteria nitrogen fixation mechanism:** Nitrogenase enzyme complex (Fe protein + MoFe protein) reduces N2 to 2NH3, consuming 16 ATP per N2. Nitrogenase is O2-sensitive. Heterocysts: thick glycolipid wall limits O2 diffusion, lack PSII (no O2 evolution), upregulate glycolysis/respiration to consume O2, fix N2, export glutamine to vegetative cells via plasmodesmata. Non-heterocystous cyanobacteria fix N2 temporally (at night) or spatially (in specialized cells).

**Viral replication strategies (Baltimore groups):** Group I: dsDNA (adenovirus, herpesvirus) — replicate in nucleus using host/viral DNA pol. Group II: ssDNA (parvovirus) — convert to dsDNA then replicate. Group III: dsRNA (reovirus) — RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in capsid transcribes mRNA. Group IV: (+)ssRNA (poliovirus, coronavirus) — genome acts as mRNA, translates RdRp, makes (-) strand template. Group V: (-)ssRNA (influenza, rabies) — virion carries RdRp to make (+) mRNA. Group VI: (+)ssRNA-RT (retroviruses, HIV) — reverse transcriptase makes dsDNA, integrates as provirus. Group VII: dsDNA-RT (hepatitis B) — RNA intermediate reverse transcribed.

**Bacteriophage applications:** Phage therapy (targeted killing of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA). Phage display (library of peptides on phage coat proteins for antibody/ligand discovery). Phage typing (epidemiological tracking of bacterial strains). Genetic engineering vectors (phage λ, M13, φX174). CRISPR-Cas systems originated as bacterial anti-phage defense.

**Antibiotic mechanisms targeting bacteria:** β-lactams (penicillin) inhibit transpeptidase crosslinking peptidoglycan. Glycopeptides (vancomycin) bind D-Ala-D-Ala termini. Aminoglycosides (streptomycin) bind 30S ribosomal subunit causing misreading. Macrolides (erythromycin) bind 50S subunit blocking translocation. Tetracyclines block tRNA entry at 30S. Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. Sulfonamides/trimethoprim block folate synthesis. Rifampin inhibits RNA polymerase.

**Viral immune evasion strategies:** Antigenic drift (point mutations in HA/NA of influenza) and shift (reassortment of segmented genome). Latency (herpesviruses establish lifelong latency in neurons/lymphocytes). Downregulation of MHC class I (adenovirus, CMV, HIV) to evade CD8+ T cells. Interference with interferon signaling (influenza NS1, SARS-CoV-2 ORF proteins). Molecular mimicry of host proteins. Rapid mutation (HIV RT error-prone, no proofreading).

**Bacterial biofilms and quorum sensing:** Biofilms = structured communities in extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix. Up to 1000x more antibiotic resistant than planktonic cells. Quorum sensing: autoinducers (AHLs in Gram-positive, AI-2 in both) accumulate at high density, bind receptors, regulate virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence (Vibrio fischeri). Interspecies communication via AI-2. Biofilms critical in chronic infections (cystic fibrosis, catheter infections, dental plaque).

**Cyanobacteria toxins and harmful algal blooms (HABs):** Microcystins (hepatotoxins, inhibit protein phosphatases), nodularins, cylindrospermopsin (hepatotoxin), anatoxin-a (neurotoxin, nicotinic agonist), saxitoxins (neurotoxins, block Na+ channels). Eutrophication (N/P runoff from agriculture) triggers blooms. WHO guideline: 1 μg/L microcystin-LR in drinking water. Blooms cause fish kills, contaminate water supplies, threaten livestock/pets/humans.
confusion: Do not confuse this concept with similar-sounding terms. Check definitions carefully.
Always verify the conditions under which the formula applies — many formulas have restricted domains.
Sign conventions matter. Define your coordinate system before applying equations.
Bacteria are prokaryotes (no nucleus) — viruses are NOT cells at all; they are acellular particles. Do not classify viruses as prokaryotes or eukaryotes.
Cyanobacteria are bacteria (Monera), NOT algae (which are eukaryotic protists). The name 'blue-green algae' is a misnomer — they are photosynthetic bacteria.
Gram-positive does NOT mean 'more pathogenic' — it describes cell wall structure. Many Gram-positive bacteria are harmless or beneficial.
Lysogenic cycle does NOT kill the host immediately — the prophage replicates silently with the host. Induction (triggered by stress) converts it to lytic cycle.

Binary fission is NOT the same as mitosis. Binary fission occurs in prokaryotes and does not involve spindle fibers, nuclear envelope breakdown, or chromosome condensation visible under light microscope.
Antibiotics target bacterial structures (cell wall, 70S ribosomes, folate synthesis) — they DO NOT work against viruses because viruses lack these structures.
Not all bacteria are harmful — the vast majority are beneficial or neutral. Only ~1% of known bacteria are pathogenic. Human microbiome bacteria are essential for health.

Viral envelopes are derived from host cell membranes (nuclear, ER, Golgi, or plasma membrane) but contain VIRAL glycoproteins. The lipid composition matches the host, but spike proteins are virus-encoded.

Bacteriophages are viruses that infect BACTERIA only — they cannot infect eukaryotic cells. Phage therapy exploits this specificity to target pathogens without harming human cells or beneficial microbiota.
Endospores are for SURVIVAL not reproduction — one vegetative cell forms one endospore, which later germinates into one vegetative cell. No increase in number occurs.
Cyanobacteria do NOT have chloroplasts — they perform photosynthesis in thylakoid membranes free in the cytoplasm. Chloroplasts evolved from endosymbiotic cyanobacteria ~1.5 billion years ago.

The lytic cycle ALWAYS ends in host cell lysis and death. The lysogenic cycle may remain dormant indefinitely. Some phages are ONLY lytic (virulent phages like T4); others are temperate (can do both, like λ phage).

Archaea are NOT just 'extreme bacteria' — they are a separate domain of life with unique biochemistry (ether lipids, different transcription/translation machinery more similar to eukaryotes). Many live in moderate environments.

Prions are NOT viruses — they contain no nucleic acid at all, only misfolded protein. They are resistant to all methods that destroy nucleic acids (UV, nucleases) but can be inactivated by protein denaturation.

Conjugation is NOT sexual reproduction — it transfers genetic material but does not produce offspring. It is horizontal gene transfer, not vertical inheritance. The donor cell (F+) remains F+ after transfer.
Viroids are NOT viruses — they lack a protein coat entirely and consist only of circular single-stranded RNA. They infect plants only, not animals.

Quorum sensing is NOT just 'bacteria talking' — it is a precise chemical communication system where autoinducer concentration directly correlates with population density, triggering coordinated gene expression changes.
practice: Solve one basic problem using the key formula from this topic.
Try a numerical problem where you must choose the correct formula from two similar options.
Apply this concept to a real-world situation and explain each step.
A culture of E. coli doubles every 20 minutes starting with 100 cells. Calculate the population after 2 hours, 4 hours, and 8 hours. At what point would resources become limiting?
Describe how you would distinguish between a Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterium under a microscope. Explain the structural basis for the staining difference.
Compare and contrast the lytic and lysogenic cycles of a bacteriophage. Include a diagram description of each stage and explain the biological significance of lysogeny.
Why are viruses considered obligate intracellular parasites? Explain what they lack that prevents independent reproduction and how they compensate for these deficiencies.

Cyanobacterial blooms are a growing environmental concern. Explain the mechanism of bloom formation, why they are dangerous (microcystins, oxygen depletion), and how they connect to human activity (fertilizer runoff).

A bacterial culture has a generation time of 30 minutes. Starting with 500 cells, how many cells will be present after 5 hours? If the carrying capacity of the medium is 10^9 cells/mL, after how many hours will the culture enter stationary phase?

Explain the structural differences between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cell walls that lead to different Gram staining results. Why is this distinction clinically important for antibiotic selection?
Describe the Baltimore classification system for viruses. Give one example of a virus from each of the seven groups and explain its replication strategy briefly.

Compare the nitrogen fixation strategies of heterocystous cyanobacteria (e.g., Anabaena) vs. non-heterocystous cyanobacteria (e.g., Trichodesmium). How do they solve the oxygen sensitivity problem of nitrogenase?
Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections. Describe three specific viral features that make them resistant to traditional antibiotic mechanisms.

A bacteriophage has a burst size of 200 virions per infected cell and a latent period of 30 minutes. If you infect 10^6 bacteria with 10^4 phage particles (MOI = 0.01), calculate the phage titer after two complete lytic cycles assuming all progeny successfully infect new cells.

A bacterial culture starts at 10^3 cells/mL with a generation time of 25 minutes. Calculate the time required to reach 10^9 cells/mL (carrying capacity). What phase of growth would this culture be in at each time point?

Design an experiment to determine whether a newly isolated bacterium is Gram-positive or Gram-negative, autotrophic or heterotrophic, and whether it can form endospores. What staining techniques and culture conditions would you use?

Explain how horizontal gene transfer (transformation, transduction, conjugation) contributes to the spread of antibiotic resistance in bacterial populations. Give a specific example of each mechanism.

A patient presents with a bacterial infection. Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods. The bacteria form biofilms on catheters. Describe the structural features that make these biofilms particularly treatment-resistant and what therapeutic strategies could overcome this.

Compare and contrast the replication strategies of (+)ssRNA viruses (e.g., poliovirus), (-)ssRNA viruses (e.g., influenza), and retroviruses (e.g., HIV). Why do (-)ssRNA and retroviruses need to carry polymerases in the virion while (+)ssRNA viruses do not?
universalFacts: This concept is fundamental and appears in multiple contexts across the subject.
Understanding the derivation helps more than memorizing the final formula.
Always check units and dimensions when applying this concept.
There are more bacteria in a single gram of soil (~100 million) than there are humans on Earth (~8 billion).
Bacteriophages are the most abundant biological entities on Earth — estimated 10³¹ particles, exceeding bacterial numbers 10:1.
The human body contains roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells (~38 trillion each), mostly in the gut. These microbiome bacteria are essential for digestion, immunity, and mental health.
Viruses likely originated multiple times independently — some may be degenerate cells, others escaped genetic elements. Their exact origin remains one of biology's unsolved mysteries.
Cyanobacteria invented oxygenic photosynthesis ~2.4 billion years ago, causing the Great Oxidation Event that transformed Earth's atmosphere and enabled complex life.
The bacterial flagellar motor is a nanomachine that rotates at up to 100,000 RPM, powered by proton motive force — one of the most efficient molecular motors known.
Some viruses (mimiviruses) have genomes larger than some bacteria (Mycoplasma genitalium, 580 kbp) and encode their own translation components, challenging the definition of life.
Bacterial conjugation can transfer chromosomal DNA (Hfr strains) or plasmids (F+ strains). The F plasmid can integrate into the chromosome, turning the cell into an Hfr donor.

CRISPR-Cas systems provide adaptive immunity in bacteria/archaea against phages. Spacers from phage DNA are incorporated into CRISPR array, transcribed as crRNA, guiding Cas proteins to cleave invading phage DNA.

Viroids are infectious agents even simpler than viruses — just small circular ssRNA (250-400 nt) with no protein coat, replicating via host RNA polymerase. Cause plant diseases (potato spindle tuber viroid).

Prions are infectious proteins (no nucleic acid) — misfolded PrP^Sc converts normal PrP^C into more PrP^Sc. Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (mad cow disease, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease).
